preferred: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q8h; may add azithromycin 500 mg IV/PO q24h for 3 days or doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h when atypical coverage is indicated
alternative: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h
If Pseudomonas risk: piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8h
recommendations.duration: Usual severe CAP 5–7 days; antipseudomonal regimen 7 days.

why: Current NAG also emphasizes local antibiogram and pseudomonal risk before antipseudomonal therapy; open the live NAG page for the latest national wording.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: Severe community-acquired pneumonia results from lower-respiratory invasion with intense host inflammatory response; pathogen spectrum changes with structural lung disease, post-influenza disease and other risk factors.

conditions.name: Severe Malaria
conditions.summary: Parenteral artesunate is the preferred severe-malaria therapy in the MSIC source, with species-specific follow-on/eradication therapy.
before: Confirm parasitaemia/species where possible but do not delay severe-malaria treatment
Check glucose, haemolysis, renal and neurologic complications
Review pregnancy and G6PD status before species-specific adjuncts such as primaquine

recommendations.label: Severe malaria
preferred: Artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV at 0, 12 and 24 h, then q24h while parenteral therapy remains required
alternative: Quinine dihydrochloride 20 mg/kg IV loading over 4 h, then 10 mg/kg q8h when artesunate is unavailable, with the source-listed companion therapy
recommendations.duration: Transition to oral ACT when clinically able; complete species-specific therapy.

why: Severe malaria is a time-critical multisystem emergency; antimalarial treatment runs in parallel with organ support.
conditions.diseaseMechanism: High parasite biomass, haemolysis, microvascular sequestration and host inflammatory responses drive multiorgan dysfunction in severe malaria.

conditions.name: Spinal Epidural Abscess
conditions.summary: Urgent diagnosis, source control/neurosurgical assessment and prolonged pathogen-directed therapy are required.
before: Obtain appropriate microbiology before antimicrobial therapy when this will not cause harmful delay
Review previous cultures and recent antimicrobial exposure
Check allergy, renal function and interacting/toxic co-medications
Assess source control and severity
Urgent MRI and surgical/neurosurgical assessment when neurological compromise or drainable collection is suspected

recommendations.label: Empirical staphylococcal coverage
preferred: Cloxacillin 2 g IV q6h
alternative: Add/replace with vancomycin when MRSA risk is important or the patient deteriorates
recommendations.duration: Usually ≥6 weeks; NAG notes at least an initial IV phase, modified by source control and response.

why: Neurological deterioration and inadequate source control can produce irreversible harm.

conditions.name: Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis
conditions.summary: Ascitic-fluid infection in cirrhosis. Diagnostic paracentesis, cultures and early therapy are central; distinguish primary SBP from secondary peritonitis.
before: Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic cell count/differential
Inoculate ascitic fluid into blood culture bottles at bedside when possible
Obtain blood cultures in septic patients
Assess for secondary peritonitis/source-control features

recommendations.label: Primary SBP — national pathway
preferred: Cefotaxime 2 g IV q8h OR ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h
alternative: Amoxicillin–clavulanate 1.2 g IV q6h OR ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV q12h
recommendations.duration: 5–7 days; IV→PO ciprofloxacin may be considered when clinically appropriate.

recommendations.label: ICU principle
preferred: Treat when ascitic PMN count is ≥250 cells/mm³ in the appropriate clinical context; bedside inoculation into blood culture bottles improves culture yield.
recommendations.duration: Tailor to response and microbiology.

why: A positive culture is not required to start therapy when the clinical/ascitic neutrophil criteria support SBP.

conditions.name: Suspected HSV Encephalitis
conditions.summary: Treat suspected HSV encephalitis promptly while diagnostic CSF/PCR and neuroimaging evaluation proceeds.
before: Obtain CSF/PCR when safe without delaying therapy
Check renal function and weight used for acyclovir dosing
Review need for neuroimaging before lumbar puncture

recommendations.label: Empirical HSV coverage
preferred: Acyclovir 10 mg/kg IV q8h
alternative: Adjust interval for renal impairment
recommendations.duration: Usually 14–21 days; use virologic/clinical response and specialist guidance.

why: Acyclovir is time-critical when HSV encephalitis is suspected; renal adjustment is central to safe therapy.

conditions.name: Systemic Brucellosis
conditions.summary: Combination therapy is required to reduce relapse; focal disease and pregnancy require modified regimens.
before: Confirm occupational/food/animal exposure
Obtain blood cultures/serology and assess focal complications including endocarditis/neurobrucellosis

recommendations.label: Systemic disease
preferred: Doxycycline 100 mg PO q12h × 6 weeks + gentamicin 5 mg/kg/day for the initial 7 days
alternative: Streptomycin 1 g IM daily for 2–3 weeks can replace gentamicin in a source-listed regimen; rifampicin-containing alternatives exist
recommendations.duration: Combination therapy commonly 6 weeks; focal disease is longer.

why: Monotherapy carries a higher relapse risk.

conditions.name: Tetanus
conditions.summary: Management combines wound debridement, toxin neutralisation, antimicrobial therapy and intensive supportive control of spasms/autonomic dysfunction.
before: Immediate wound assessment/debridement
Administer tetanus immune globulin and initiate active immunisation as indicated
Prepare airway/autonomic supportive care for severe disease

recommendations.label: Antimicrobial component
preferred: Metronidazole 500 mg IV q6–8h
alternative: Benzylpenicillin is a source-listed alternative
recommendations.duration: Approximately 7–10 days in the NAG pathway; immune globulin and wound management are separate essential components.

why: Antibiotics stop bacterial proliferation but do not neutralise toxin already bound to neural tissue.

conditions.name: Toxoplasma Encephalitis
conditions.summary: Use a complete anti-toxoplasma combination regimen and treat long enough for clinical/radiologic response.
before: Confirm HIV/immunocompromised context
Review brain imaging and differential diagnosis
Check marrow/renal baseline before folate-antagonist therapy

recommendations.label: Preferred source-listed options
preferred: Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole using TMP 10 mg/kg/day divided q12h OR pyrimethamine-based combination + folinic acid + sulfadiazine
alternative: Clindamycin-containing alternative when sulfadiazine cannot be used
recommendations.duration: At least 6 weeks, then secondary prophylaxis according to host response.

why: Combination therapy and folinic acid rescue are integral to the pyrimethamine regimen.

conditions.name: Typhoid Fever
conditions.summary: Use susceptibility testing and local resistance data; XDR disease changes treatment.
before: Obtain cultures before therapy when feasible
Assess severity and complications
Review travel/exposure and resistance/susceptibility

recommendations.label: Mild adult typhoid
preferred: Ceftriaxone 2–4 g/day IV divided q12–24h OR cefotaxime 2–6 g/day IV divided q8–12h
alternative: Ciprofloxacin or azithromycin only according to susceptibility/result and source pathway
recommendations.duration: Minimum 7–14 days; IV→PO when improving and an active oral option is available.

recommendations.label: XDR / resistant severe disease
preferred: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h in the NAG XDR pathway
alternative: Use susceptibility and ID/microbiology guidance.
recommendations.duration: Source-/response-specific; verify live NAG.

conditions.name: Uncomplicated Lower Urinary Tract Infection
conditions.summary: Use a lower-tract regimen guided by current NAG/local susceptibility and avoid agents that do not achieve appropriate urinary activity.
before: Confirm lower-tract symptoms without systemic/upper-tract features
Check pregnancy status, renal function and prior resistant urine cultures

recommendations.label: Uncomplicated cystitis
preferred: Nitrofurantoin or other NAG-listed lower-tract agent based on current local pathway
alternative: Fosfomycin 3 g PO single dose in selected patients; reliability is mainly for E. coli in this context
recommendations.duration: Agent-specific; check latest NAG UTI page.

why: Lower-tract therapy should not be extrapolated to pyelonephritis or systemic infection.

conditions.name: Urosepsis
conditions.summary: Treat sepsis and assess for obstructed infected urinary tract, which requires urgent source control.
before: Blood cultures and urine culture
Assess urinary obstruction/stone and need for urgent drainage
Review previous urinary isolates and ESBL/CRE risk
Check renal function

recommendations.label: Local empirical regimen
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q8h
alternative: Cefepime 1 g IV q8h
recommendations.duration: 10–14 days in the source

recommendations.label: Without shock
preferred: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q24h OR cefotaxime 2 g IV q8h
alternative: Ceftazidime 2 g IV q8h OR cefepime 2 g IV q8h
recommendations.duration: ≥7 days; early urinary source control is a core treatment principle.

recommendations.label: With shock
preferred: Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8h
alternative: Meropenem 1 g IV q8h OR imipenem 500 mg IV q6h
recommendations.duration: ≥7 days; choose according to severity, resistance risk and local antibiogram, with early source control.

organisms.name: Acinetobacter baumannii
notes: Common ICU healthcare-associated pathogen; colonisation is frequent, so infection-vs-colonisation assessment is essential.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Environmental organism that persists on hospital surfaces and equipment; colonises skin/respiratory tract in some patients.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Low intrinsic virulence but strong environmental persistence, biofilm formation and multidrug resistance permit severe infection in vulnerable ICU hosts.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Distinguish colonisation from true infection; CRAB phenotype drives therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Aerobic, non-fermenting Gram-negative coccobacillus with environmental persistence.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Carbapenem resistance is common in CRAB and often coexists with resistance across multiple antimicrobial classes.

organisms.name: Burkholderia pseudomallei
notes: Treatment has an intensive phase and prolonged eradication phase.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Soil and surface water in endemic tropical regions; inoculation, inhalation and ingestion are recognised routes.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Facultative intracellular survival, multiple secretion systems and abscess formation allow latent, relapsing and disseminated melioidosis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Treatment requires intensive and eradication phases; source control and relapse prevention matter.

organisms.name: Candida spp.
notes: Colonisation is common in ICU patients; invasive disease must be distinguished from colonisation.

microbiology.familyOrGroup: Ascomycetous yeasts; family varies by species
microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal coloniser of gastrointestinal/skin/mucosal sites; invasive disease follows barrier disruption, broad antibiotics and critical illness.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Adhesion, biofilm formation and host-barrier failure allow candidaemia and deep-seated candidiasis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Colonisation alone is common in ICU patients and is not equivalent to invasive candidiasis.

organisms.name: Citrobacter freundii
notes: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in the MSIDC consensus.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal/environmental organism.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Can express inducible chromosomal AmpC, creating clinically significant resistance during therapy.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in MSIDC guidance.

organisms.name: Clostridioides difficile
notes: Antibiotic exposure is a major risk; treatment is severity- and recurrence-specific.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Spores persist in healthcare/community environments; colonises the colon after microbiome disruption.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Toxins A/B damage colonic epithelium and drive inflammation, diarrhoea and pseudomembranous colitis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Do not test/treat asymptomatic colonisation; severity and recurrence history determine therapy.

organisms.name: Cryptococcus neoformans
notes: Raised intracranial pressure management is central in cryptococcal meningitis.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Environmental encapsulated yeast; infection follows inhalation with later dissemination, especially in impaired cellular immunity.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Polysaccharide capsule and melanin help evade host defences; CNS tropism produces meningitis and raised intracranial pressure.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Management includes antifungal phases plus aggressive intracranial-pressure assessment/control.

organisms.name: Enterobacter cloacae complex
notes: MSIDC places Enterobacter cloacae complex among moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organisms.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal/environmental organism and healthcare-associated opportunist.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Chromosomal inducible AmpC can be derepressed during β-lactam exposure, producing on-therapy resistance to some cephalosporins.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in MSIDC guidance.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal gastrointestinal flora; healthcare transmission is important for resistant strains.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Intrinsic and acquired resistance plus tolerance of harsh environments facilitate device, urinary and bloodstream infection in vulnerable hosts.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Species and vancomycin susceptibility matter; E. faecium is generally more resistant than E. faecalis.
microbiology.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in pairs/chains; hardy gastrointestinal commensals.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Intrinsic cephalosporin resistance and acquired vancomycin resistance (VRE) are key therapeutic issues.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Normal gastrointestinal flora; extra-intestinal strains cause ascending urinary and invasive infection.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Virulence varies by pathotype; adhesins, capsules, toxins and siderophores contribute to urinary, intestinal and bloodstream disease.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: ESBL and CRE mechanisms can radically change therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod in Enterobacterales; common gut commensal.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: ESBL and carbapenemase acquisition changes treatment; urinary pathotypes possess adhesins that facilitate ascending UTI.

organisms.name: Haemophilus influenzae
notes: Common respiratory pathogen; invasive disease and respiratory infection use different dosing contexts.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human upper respiratory tract; spread by respiratory droplets.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Encapsulated strains evade phagocytosis; non-typeable strains commonly cause mucosal respiratory disease.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: β-lactamase production changes ampicillin/amoxicillin susceptibility.

organisms.name: Helicobacter pylori
notes: Eradication requires a complete multidrug regimen rather than single-drug therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human gastric colonisation; transmission is mainly person-to-person.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Urease buffers gastric acid; flagella/mucosal adherence and virulence proteins drive chronic gastritis and ulcer/cancer risk.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Treatment should follow current eradication regimens and local macrolide resistance context.

organisms.name: Klebsiella aerogenes
notes: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in the MSIDC consensus.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal/environmental healthcare opportunist.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Inducible chromosomal AmpC can be derepressed after β-lactam exposure.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organism in MSIDC guidance.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal/oropharyngeal colonisation with healthcare spread in high-risk settings.
microbiology.pathogenesis: A prominent polysaccharide capsule, siderophores and hypervirulent clones contribute to invasive disease; ESBL/carbapenemases drive treatment failure.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Ask whether the isolate is ESBL/CRE and, for CRE, whether a carbapenemase/MBL is known.
microbiology.morphology: Encapsulated, lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod in Enterobacterales.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: ESBL and carbapenemases (including NDM/MBL, KPC and OXA-48-like) are clinically important resistance mechanisms.

organisms.name: Leptospira spp.
notes: Severe disease may include AKI, pulmonary haemorrhage, shock and arrhythmia.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Animal renal carriage with urine contamination of water/soil; infection follows skin/mucosal exposure.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Spirochaetaemia followed by endothelial/organ injury can produce jaundice, AKI, haemorrhage and pulmonary disease.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Treat compatible severe disease promptly; diagnostic serology may be negative early.

organisms.name: Listeria monocytogenes
notes: Consider in older, pregnant and immunocompromised hosts in meningitis pathways.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Food/environmental organism with gastrointestinal entry; higher risk in pregnancy, older adults and impaired cellular immunity.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Intracellular survival and actin-mediated cell-to-cell spread enable CNS and invasive disease.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Cephalosporins are intrinsically ineffective; ampicillin/benzylpenicillin is central in susceptible disease.

organisms.name: Neisseria meningitidis
notes: Meningococcal disease requires urgent therapy and public-health/contact prophylaxis considerations.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human nasopharynx; droplet spread and close-contact transmission.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Capsule enables bloodstream survival; endotoxin-driven inflammation can cause fulminant meningococcaemia and shock.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Rapid public-health/contact prophylaxis assessment is part of management.

organisms.name: Pneumocystis jirovecii
notes: Host immune status and oxygenation determine treatment intensity and steroid indication.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human respiratory organism; disease occurs predominantly with impaired cellular immunity.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Alveolar fungal proliferation triggers diffuse interstitial inflammation and severe gas-exchange impairment.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Assess hypoxaemia because adjunctive corticosteroid criteria depend on severity in HIV-associated PJP.

organisms.name: Proteus mirabilis
notes: Common urinary pathogen; resistance phenotype and renal function guide therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Gastrointestinal flora; ascending urinary infection is common.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Strong urease activity alkalinises urine and promotes struvite stone formation and catheter encrustation.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Intrinsic reduced susceptibility to some agents and urinary tract anatomy/stones matter.

organisms.name: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
notes: Expected-spectrum table includes activity from selected antipseudomonal β-lactams and aminoglycosides; susceptibility testing remains decisive.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Soil/water and moist healthcare reservoirs such as sinks and respiratory equipment.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Opportunistic invasion is supported by biofilm/alginate, exotoxin A, endotoxin, secreted enzymes and impaired host defences; resistance often involves permeability/efflux/AmpC mechanisms.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Resistance phenotype matters more than the organism name alone; DTR is a treatment-limiting phenotype.
microbiology.morphology: Aerobic, non-fermenting Gram-negative rod; oxidase positive; forms biofilm.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Intrinsic and acquired mechanisms include low permeability, efflux, inducible/chromosomal AmpC and OprD changes; DTR phenotype should drive treatment selection.

organisms.name: Salmonella Typhi
notes: Travel/geography and susceptibility pattern materially change therapy.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Humans are the reservoir; faeco-oral transmission via contaminated food/water.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Invades intestinal mucosa, survives in macrophages and disseminates through the reticuloendothelial system.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Travel/exposure history and susceptibility are important because fluoroquinolone resistance is common in many regions.

organisms.name: Serratia marcescens
notes: MSIDC describes a lower risk of clinically significant inducible AmpC than Enterobacter cloacae complex/K. aerogenes/C. freundii.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Environmental and gastrointestinal organism associated with healthcare reservoirs/devices.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Opportunistic invasion and intrinsic/acquired resistance mechanisms can complicate device and bloodstream infection.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: MSIDC categorises Serratia as lower risk for clinically significant inducible AmpC than Enterobacter cloacae complex/K. aerogenes/C. freundii.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Colonises skin and anterior nares; spreads by direct/contact transmission and can seed the bloodstream from skin/device sources.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Adhesins, immune-evasion mechanisms, coagulase and multiple toxins allow abscess formation, tissue injury and metastatic infection.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Persistent S. aureus bacteraemia requires active search for source/metastatic foci; MSSA and MRSA require different definitive therapy.
microbiology.morphology: Gram-positive cocci in clusters; catalase/coagulase positive.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: MRSA expresses altered PBP2a-mediated β-lactam resistance; MSSA should preferentially receive an active antistaphylococcal β-lactam when feasible.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Water, sinks, fomites, plants and hospital equipment.
microbiology.pathogenesis: Usually low-virulence/opportunistic; infection occurs in immunocompromised or chronically ill hosts. Intrinsic β-lactam/carbapenem resistance is a major clinical feature.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Many respiratory isolates are colonisers; do not treat colonisation.
microbiology.morphology: Aerobic non-fermenting Gram-negative rod associated with water and healthcare environments.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Intrinsic multidrug resistance includes β-lactamases and efflux; carbapenems are intrinsically ineffective and colonisation is common.

organisms.name: Streptococcus pneumoniae
notes: Major CAP/meningitis pathogen; site-specific breakpoints and CNS dosing matter.

microbiology.reservoirTransmission: Human nasopharyngeal coloniser transmitted by respiratory droplets.
microbiology.pathogenesis: The polysaccharide capsule is the principal antiphagocytic virulence factor; mucosal barrier disruption allows pneumonia, bacteraemia and meningitis.
microbiology.clinicalPearl: Asplenia and impaired humoral immunity increase invasive disease risk.
microbiology.morphology: Lancet-shaped Gram-positive diplococcus; alpha-haemolytic and encapsulated.
microbiology.resistanceSummary: Capsule is a major virulence determinant; β-lactam susceptibility varies and site-specific breakpoints matter, especially in meningitis.

resistance.name: AmpC β-Lactamase-Producing Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: AmpC risk changes interpretation of β-lactam susceptibility. Site and susceptibility determine whether cefepime or a carbapenem is preferred.

sourceCards.title: Moderate inducible AmpC risk — urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Uncomplicated cystitis: use a susceptible lower-tract option such as nitrofurantoin/TMP-SMX or a single aminoglycoside; pyelonephritis/cUTI: TMP-SMX, once-daily aminoglycoside with TDM, or cefepime are source-listed options.
bullets: Confirm susceptibility before choosing definitive therapy.
Fluoroquinolone is a less-preferred option when susceptible.

sourceCards.title: Outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Cefepime is a key preferred option when susceptible; high-inoculum/severe disease and reduced cefepime susceptibility may shift therapy toward a carbapenem.
bullets: Piperacillin–tazobactam is not recommended for moderate/high-risk inducible AmpC organisms in the dedicated consensus.

resistance.name: Carbapenem-Resistant Acinetobacter baumannii
resistance.summary: CRAB management requires infection-vs-colonisation assessment, high-dose sulbactam-based therapy in many Malaysian regimens, severity stratification and susceptibility review.

sourceCards.title: Local targeted CRAB
sourceCards.text: HPUSM uses ampicillin–sulbactam for susceptible mild disease and high-dose 9 g q8h extended infusion for moderate–severe disease, with additional agents according to severity/approval.

sourceCards.title: Dedicated CRAB algorithm
sourceCards.text: Do not treat colonisation. High-dose sulbactam-based therapy is central when treating true infection; moderate–severe disease generally uses combination therapy.
bullets: Selected companion options include minocycline or polymyxin B; colistin is favoured over polymyxin B when urinary exposure is required.
Nebulised polymyxin is not recommended routinely.
Meropenem + colistin has not shown superiority; avoid routine triple meropenem/polymyxin/ampicillin–sulbactam.

resistance.name: Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: CRE is heterogeneous. Determine whether carbapenemase is present and identify the enzyme (e.g. NDM/MBL, KPC, OXA-48-like) because this can change active options.

sourceCards.title: Non-CP CRE with retained meropenem/imipenem susceptibility
sourceCards.text: Use high-dose meropenem or imipenem with 3–4 h extended infusion when the source MIC criteria are satisfied.

sourceCards.title: CRE outside urinary tract — ceftazidime/avibactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: Ceftazidime–avibactam is preferred. Cefiderocol, high-dose tigecycline or polymyxin B are less-preferred source-listed alternatives; combination strategies are reserved for selected severe/high-burden scenarios.

sourceCards.title: Presumed/confirmed NDM
sourceCards.text: Preferred: ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam administered simultaneously, OR cefiderocol.
bullets: Consider high-dose extended-infusion meropenem as a companion only when MIC ≤8 mg/L in the source-defined combination context.

resistance.name: ESBL-Producing Enterobacterales
resistance.summary: Extended-spectrum β-lactamase phenotype. Treatment depends on infection site, severity and susceptibility; avoid treating the resistance label without the clinical syndrome.

sourceCards.title: Local severe/critical illness signal
sourceCards.text: HPUSM uses ertapenem for selected severe ESBL infection and meropenem/imipenem for critically ill/intubated ICU patients; hypoalbuminaemia and infection site alter the choice.

sourceCards.title: Uncomplicated cystitis / pyelonephritis-cUTI
sourceCards.text: Use susceptible oral/lower-tract options for uncomplicated cystitis; for pyelonephritis/cUTI, TMP-SMX or ciprofloxacin are preferred when susceptible, with aminoglycoside/carbapenem alternatives in selected cases.
bullets: Avoid unnecessary carbapenem exposure when a reliable active narrower option exists.

sourceCards.title: Infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Carbapenem is the preferred class in the dedicated MSIDC guidance; in critically ill patients or marked hypoalbuminaemia, meropenem/imipenem is favoured over ertapenem.
bullets: Piperacillin–tazobactam and cefepime are not recommended as definitive ESBL therapy outside narrow exceptions described in the source.

resistance.name: KPC-Producing CRE
resistance.summary: Carbapenemase-producing CRE with a serine carbapenemase mechanism. Therapy should be susceptibility- and site-directed using dedicated CRE guidance.

sourceCards.title: If ceftazidime–avibactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: For CRE infection outside the urinary tract, MSIDC lists ceftazidime–avibactam as the preferred option when susceptible.
bullets: Use ID/clinical microbiology review for severe/high-burden infection.

resistance.name: MDR / DTR Pseudomonas aeruginosa
resistance.summary: Use site, severity and in-vitro activity. DTR Pseudomonas should trigger dedicated MDR guidance rather than automatic carbapenem escalation.

sourceCards.title: MDR Pseudomonas, carbapenem non-susceptible but traditional β-lactam susceptible
sourceCards.text: Prefer susceptible ceftazidime, cefepime or piperacillin–tazobactam using high-dose extended infusion.

sourceCards.title: DTR Pseudomonas — cystitis / cUTI
sourceCards.text: Preferred newer β-lactams are ceftolozane–tazobactam or ceftazidime–avibactam when susceptible; site-specific alternatives include amikacin, colistin or cefiderocol.

sourceCards.title: DTR Pseudomonas — infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: Prefer ceftolozane–tazobactam or ceftazidime–avibactam. Cefiderocol or polymyxin B + a second susceptible agent are less-preferred source options.
bullets: MSIDC does not recommend routine combination therapy when an optimal active agent is available.
Nebulised antibiotics are not recommended in the cited respiratory DTR-Pseudomonas guidance.

resistance.name: Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus
resistance.summary: MRSA is resistant to usual antistaphylococcal β-lactams because of altered PBP2a. Use local MRSA risk/prevalence and syndrome severity to decide empirical coverage.

sourceCards.title: Local guidance
sourceCards.text: HPUSM recommends vancomycin for empirical therapy when MRSA risk is high/severe and for confirmed MRSA; it states vancomycin is inferior to cloxacillin for MSSA.

resistance.name: Methicillin-Susceptible Staphylococcus aureus
resistance.summary: HPUSM notes MSSA causes community and hospital-acquired bloodstream/invasive infection and that vancomycin is inferior to anti-staphylococcal penicillins such as cloxacillin for MSSA.

sourceCards.title: Local HPUSM principle
sourceCards.text: Use an anti-staphylococcal penicillin such as cloxacillin for susceptible S. aureus rather than continuing vancomycin solely for convenience; complicated MSSA infection warrants ID consultation.

resistance.name: NDM / Metallo-β-Lactamase Producing CRE
resistance.summary: Metallo-β-lactamase-producing CRE require a different strategy from KPC/OXA-48-like disease because avibactam does not inhibit the MBL itself.

sourceCards.title: Presumed/confirmed NDM — infection outside urinary tract
sourceCards.text: MSIDC lists ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam given simultaneously as a preferred regimen, or cefiderocol as another preferred option.
bullets: Tigecycline high dose or polymyxin B are less-preferred alternatives in the source.
Avoid high-dose tigecycline for bacteraemia in the cited pathway.

resistance.name: Non-Carbapenemase-Producing CRE
resistance.summary: CRE can result from non-carbapenemase β-lactamase activity plus permeability changes. Some isolates remain susceptible to meropenem/imipenem despite ertapenem resistance.

sourceCards.title: Meropenem/imipenem susceptible non-CP CRE
sourceCards.text: If meropenem and imipenem MICs remain ≤1 µg/mL with ertapenem non-susceptibility, MSIDC recommends high-dose meropenem or imipenem using 3–4 h extended infusion.

resistance.name: OXA-48-like CRE
resistance.summary: OXA-48-like carbapenemase phenotype. Use susceptibility testing and the CRE pathway rather than assuming all carbapenems or β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitors behave alike.

sourceCards.title: CRE mechanism-directed approach
sourceCards.text: MSIDC separates carbapenemase-producing CRE by mechanism and ceftazidime–avibactam susceptibility; use the CRE treatment algorithm and AST.

resistance.name: Stenotrophomonas maltophilia
resistance.summary: Intrinsically resistant to carbapenems. Distinguish colonisation from infection and use susceptibility/site/severity to select therapy.

sourceCards.title: First question: infection or colonisation?
sourceCards.text: If the isolate represents colonisation, do not treat.

sourceCards.title: Treatment when true infection is present
sourceCards.text: TMP-SMX IV/PO is preferred. Cefiderocol or ceftazidime–avibactam PLUS aztreonam are less-preferred source-listed options.
bullets: For moderate–severe infection, the source prefers combination therapy when using TMP-SMX or cefiderocol until clinical improvement.
Levofloxacin or minocycline may serve as a susceptibility-directed companion.

sourceCards.title: Tetracycline caveat
sourceCards.text: Because minocycline/tetracycline derivatives have low urine and serum concentrations, avoid them for UTI and use only in combination for bacteraemia.

checklist: Clinical inflammatory response stable or improving
Functional GI tract and no major absorption problem
Active oral agent with suitable bioavailability/spectrum is available
No syndrome/device/source reason requiring continued IV therapy
Document total duration, stop date and follow-up plan
avoid: High-risk neutropenia/severe infection during chemotherapy-related neutropenia
Melioidosis before adequate IV intensive phase
Severely immunocompromised patient when source requires IV
notes: NAG notes that adequately drained abscess/empyema, osteomyelitis and septic arthritis may be switched after ≥2 weeks IV in appropriate improving patients.
MSIC also flags endocarditis, CNS infection and S. aureus bacteraemia as conditions not recommended for routine early IV→PO conversion.

nagSnapshot.rule: Structured NAG data are searchable offline, but every NAG-derived result retains a live link to check the official current source.

hypoalbuminaemia.name: Hypoalbuminaemia (albumin ≤25 g/L)
hypoalbuminaemia.summary: Highly protein-bound antimicrobials may have increased free fraction, volume of distribution and clearance, reducing exposure despite a higher unbound fraction.
principles: Avoid ertapenem in critically ill patients with marked hypoalbuminaemia in the cited MSIC appendix.
Use drug-specific loading/maintenance or TDM strategies rather than reducing dose solely because albumin is low.

obesity.name: Obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m²)
obesity.summary: Dosing weight depends on antimicrobial properties. Volume of distribution informs loading dose; clearance informs maintenance dose.
principles: Drug-specific obesity recommendations should supersede generic weight rules.

ecmo.name: ECMO
ecmo.summary: ECMO can alter antimicrobial pharmacokinetics through circuit sequestration, haemodilution, altered volume of distribution and drug elimination; available antibiotic dosing data are limited.
principles: Use standard/critical-illness loading exposure unless a drug-specific source states otherwise.
Prioritise TDM when available for narrow-therapeutic-index agents.

augmented-renal-clearance.name: Augmented renal clearance (ARC)
augmented-renal-clearance.summary: Critical illness can produce renal clearance above normal, risking subtherapeutic exposure for renally eliminated antimicrobials.
principles: Use measured/estimated clearance and clinical context rather than assuming normal exposure at a “normal” creatinine.
MSIDC cefiderocol table includes a higher-frequency regimen for CrCl >120 mL/min.

cns-infection.name: Central nervous system infection
cns-infection.summary: CNS infection may require higher β-lactam exposure than non-CNS infection. The MSIC renal table explicitly provides high-dose meropenem and higher-dose cefepime/ceftazidime contexts.
principles: Do not apply a standard non-CNS dose to meningitis/ventriculitis without checking the syndrome-specific source.
Renal adjustment must preserve adequate CNS exposure while reducing toxicity risk.

sources.summary: NAG: AUC/MIC is the efficacy exposure metric; TDM is indicated when vancomycin is expected for >48 h, with more frequent monitoring when PK is unstable.
MSIC provides loading, renal/RRT regimens and sampling schedules; its ICU appendix lists AUC24/MIC target 400–600.
NAG describes extended-interval/single-daily dosing and lists patient groups where it is not appropriate, including pregnancy, CrCl <30 mL/min, dialysis, endocarditis and haemodynamic instability.
MSIC provides timed level sampling for single-daily and conventional aminoglycoside dosing and recommends more frequent monitoring with changing renal function/nephrotoxins.
